subject: Biology
title: Plant Growth and Development
summary: The chapter explains how a plant grows (meristems, the three phases of growth, arithmetic and geometric growth and the sigmoid curve), how cells differentiate, dedifferentiate and redifferentiate, what plasticity means in development, and then the five groups of plant growth regulators: their discovery, chemical nature and physiological effects. It is the last chapter of Unit IV (Plant Physiology), a regular source of 1-mark, 3-mark and 5-mark questions in the Class 11 final, and one of the most reliable NEET chapters because nearly every question is a sentence from NCERT.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Plant Growth and Development belongs to Unit IV, Plant Physiology, which carries about 12 marks shared with Photosynthesis in Higher Plants and Respiration in Plants. In a typical school final this chapter alone contributes 4 to 8 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on which hormone does what, or on the discovery stories, and an Assertion-Reason on apical dominance or ABA as the stress hormone), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on arithmetic versus geometric growth, the phases of growth, or plasticity, and quite often a 5-mark question asking for the physiological effects of two or more plant growth regulators, or the sigmoid growth curve with a labelled diagram. In NEET it gives two to four questions a year, almost all on the growth regulators and the growth curves.

question_types.note: Which PGR causes bolting, fruit ripening, apical dominance, stomatal closure, parthenocarpy, or is used as a herbicide (2,4-D); the plant used in each discovery (canary grass, oat coleoptile, rice bakanae, herring sperm DNA, oranges and bananas); the scientist paired with the hormone (Darwin, Went, Kurosawa, Skoog and Miller, Cousins); the chemical class of each PGR (indole, adenine derivative, terpene, carotenoid derivative, gas); the phases of the sigmoid curve; number of new cells per hour in a maize root apex (17,500); the hormone synthesised in senescing tissues (ethylene); zeatin source (corn kernels, coconut milk).

ABA is called the stress hormone because it closes stomata and raises tolerance; cytokinins overcome apical dominance because they promote lateral bud growth; ethylene is a gas yet a PGR; growth in plants is indeterminate because meristems retain the capacity to divide; 2,4-D kills dicot weeds without affecting mature monocots; both growth and differentiation are open; relative growth rate is higher in the smaller of two leaves adding the same area.

Define growth, differentiation, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, meristem, growth rate, plasticity, apical dominance, bolting, parthenocarpy, senescence, abscission; write two differences between arithmetic and geometric growth; name the three phases of growth at a root tip; give one natural and one synthetic auxin; expand IAA, IBA, NAA, 2,4-D, GA<sub>3</sub>, ABA; name the PGR you would use for a given job (rooting, ripening, bolting, stomatal closure, delaying senescence).

Explain arithmetic growth with the equation L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + rt and a graph; explain the three phases of the sigmoid curve; absolute versus relative growth rate with the two-leaf example; the three phases of growth at the root tip with the features of cells in each; dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with the cambium example; plasticity with heterophylly examples; discovery of auxin or gibberellin or cytokinin; characteristics and chemical nature of PGRs; why ABA is the stress hormone; the 'open' form of growth; conditions for growth.

Physiological effects and agricultural uses of auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and ABA (often 'any three' or 'any two'); the whole story of the discovery of the five PGRs; arithmetic versus geometric growth with both graphs and both equations and the sigmoid curve explained; NCERT exercise question 4 (five groups of PGRs plus a note on one of them) and question 7 (which PGR for which job) as a combined question; growth, differentiation and development defined and related, with plasticity.

A gardener or farmer scenario: a rotten fruit ripening a whole basket (ethylene), a tea plantation or hedge pruned to make it bushy (apical dominance and cytokinin), sugarcane sprayed with GA, a lawn treated with 2,4-D, a plant wilting in drought and closing stomata (ABA), a tissue-culture medium lacking cytokinin; or a data-table on seedling length per day from which the student identifies arithmetic or geometric growth and calculates growth rate.

sections.heading: 13.1 Growth: definition, indeterminate growth and meristems
sections.body:
Start with the NCERT definition, because a 2-mark question can be nothing more than this. Growth is an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ or its parts, or even of an individual cell. It is generally accompanied by metabolic processes (both anabolic and catabolic) that occur at the expense of energy. Two words in the definition matter to the examiner: irreversible (a leaf swelling with water and shrinking again is not growth) and permanent. The expansion of a leaf is growth; the swelling of a wooden door in the monsoon is not, because it reverses when the wood dries.

Plant growth is generally indeterminate. Plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout their life because they have meristems at certain locations in their body. Cells of these meristems have the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate: with every division one product remains meristematic while the other becomes a body cell. Because new cells are always being added to the body by the meristem, this form of growth, in which new cells keep being added, is called the open form of growth.

Three meristems are named. The root apical meristem and the shoot apical meristem are responsible for primary growth, which mainly contributes to elongation of the plant along its axis. In dicotyledonous plants and gymnosperms, the lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and the cork cambium, appear later in life and are responsible for secondary growth, the increase in girth of the organs. Intercalary meristems (at the base of internodes and leaf sheaths in grasses) explain why a lawn regrows after mowing; NCERT mentions them in the anatomy chapter, and they are a favourite explanation in questions about grass regenerating after grazing.

Contrast this with animals, whose growth is determinate: it stops once a fixed size is reached. In a plant, even a very old tree keeps adding new leaves, roots and wood every season. That contrast, indeterminate versus determinate, is the point of NCERT exercise question 1 (define determinate growth) and of the exemplar question on why plants have an open form of growth.

formulas.expr: Growth = irreversible, permanent increase in size of an organ, part or cell, accompanied by metabolic processes at the expense of energy
where: root and shoot apical meristems; elongation along the axis
lateral meristems (vascular cambium, cork cambium); increase in girth; dicots and gymnosperms

sections.tip: Write 'irreversible permanent increase' in the definition every time; students who write 'increase in size' alone lose the mark. Give one example of what is not growth (swelling of a seed in water before it starts metabolising) if the question has a 'why' in it.

sections.heading: 13.1.2 Growth is Measurable
sections.body:
At the cellular level growth is principally a consequence of an increase in the amount of protoplasm. Because protoplasm cannot be measured directly, growth is measured through a variety of parameters, and this is the answer to NCERT exercise question 2 (why no single parameter is good enough). The parameters NCERT lists are increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number.

The three numerical examples are asked as MCQs, so learn them exactly. A maize root apical meristem can produce more than 17,500 new cells per hour: here growth is best counted as cell number. Cells in a watermelon may increase in size by up to 3,50,000 times: here growth is an increase in cell size, measured as volume. In a pollen tube growth is measured in terms of length, and in a dorsiventral leaf it is measured as increase in surface area.

The reason no single parameter serves throughout the life of a flowering plant is that different organs and different stages grow in different ways. A root elongates (length), a leaf expands (area), a fruit swells (volume), a tuber adds stored food (dry weight), a meristem adds cells (cell number). Fresh weight is easy to take but rises and falls with water content, which is why dry weight is the more reliable measure of real growth for a whole plant. So the parameter chosen must suit the organ and the stage; one measure alone would miss growth happening in another form.

Write the answer to the 'why not one parameter' question with two parts: (i) growth is basically an increase in protoplasm, which cannot be measured directly, so we use proxies; (ii) each proxy suits a particular organ or stage, with the maize, watermelon, pollen tube and leaf examples.

formulas.expr: Parameters of growth: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume, cell number
where: more than 17,500 new cells per hour (cell number)

sections.tip: The figure is 17,500 cells per hour in a maize root apex, not per day and not per minute. Examiners set the wrong unit as a distractor.

sections.heading: 13.1.3 Phases of Growth
sections.body:
The period of growth is generally divided into three phases: meristematic, elongation and maturation. NCERT illustrates them on a root tip (Fig. 13.2), and a 3-mark question usually asks you to describe the three phases with the characteristics of the cells in each. The same three phases exist in the shoot apex too.

Meristematic phase. The cells constantly dividing, both at the root apex and at the shoot apex, represent this phase. The cells in this region are rich in protoplasm and possess large, conspicuous nuclei. Their cell walls are primary in nature, thin and cellulosic, with abundant plasmodesmatal connections. These four features (dense protoplasm, large nucleus, thin primary cellulosic wall, many plasmodesmata) are the marking points; give all four.

Phase of elongation. The cells just proximal (just behind) to the meristematic zone are in this phase. It is marked by increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new cell wall deposition. The rapid lengthening of a root or stem is mostly this phase, not the meristem: a dividing cell does not get much longer, but a cell taking in water into a growing vacuole can lengthen many times.

Phase of maturation. The portion of the axis further away from the apex, proximal to the phase of elongation, represents this phase. The cells attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications. Most of the tissues and cell types we studied in the anatomy chapter (tracheids, vessels, fibres, sieve tubes) are cells in this phase. In a root the maturation zone is where root hairs appear, which is a good landmark to add to the diagram.

Notice the order from the tip backwards: division, then enlargement, then maturation. A cell passes through the three in sequence, and the three zones exist together at the same time at any tip.

formulas.expr: Root tip from the apex backwards: root cap → meristematic zone (division) → zone of elongation → zone of maturation (root hairs)
where: rich protoplasm, large nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls, abundant plasmodesmata
increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, new wall deposition
maximal size, wall thickening, protoplasmic modifications

sections.tip: If asked for a diagram, draw the root tip with the three zones labelled and write one feature of the cells beside each zone. That earns the 3 marks even if the sketch is rough.

sections.heading: 13.1.4 Growth Rates: arithmetic and geometric growth
sections.body:
The increased growth per unit time is termed the growth rate. An organism, or a part of it, can produce more cells in a variety of ways, and NCERT describes two mathematical patterns: arithmetic and geometric.

Arithmetic growth. Following mitotic cell division, only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures. The simplest expression is a root elongating at a constant rate. Plotting length against time gives a straight line (a linear curve, NCERT Fig. 13.3). Mathematically,

Lt = L0 + rt

where Lt is the length at time t, L0 is the length at time zero and r is the growth rate (elongation per unit time). Every unit of time adds the same fixed amount, so the increase is by addition.

Geometric growth. In most systems the initial growth is slow (lag phase), and it increases rapidly thereafter at an exponential rate (log or exponential phase). Here both daughter cells produced by mitosis retain the ability to divide and keep dividing. But with limited nutrient supply the growth slows down, leading to a stationary phase. If we plot the parameter of growth against time we get a typical sigmoid (S-shaped) curve (NCERT Fig. 13.4). A sigmoid curve is characteristic of a living organism growing in a natural environment, and it is typical for all cells, tissues and organs of a plant. The exponential growth can be expressed as

W1 = W0 ert

where W1 is the final size (weight, height, number etc.), W0 the initial size at the beginning of the period, r the growth rate, t the time of growth and e the base of natural logarithms. Here r is the relative growth rate, and it is also a measure of the ability of the plant to produce new plant material, referred to as the efficiency index. Hence the final size of W1 depends on the initial size, W0.

Absolute and relative growth rates. Quantitative comparisons between the growth of living systems can be made in two ways. Absolute growth rate is the measurement and comparison of total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate is the growth of the given system per unit time expressed on a common basis, for example per unit initial parameter. NCERT Fig. 13.5 shows two leaves, A and B, of different initial sizes that both add the same absolute area, 5 cm2, in a given time; the smaller leaf, which grew from 5 cm2 to 10 cm2, shows the higher relative growth rate (100 per cent) than the larger leaf, which grew from 50 cm2 to 55 cm2 (10 per cent). Same absolute growth, different relative growth: that is the whole point of the figure.

A quick worked example of the kind a case-based question may set: a root 2 cm long grows to 8 cm in 3 days. Absolute growth rate = (8 − 2)/3 = 2 cm per day. Relative growth rate = (8 − 2)/2 = 3, i.e. 300 per cent over the 3 days, or 100 per cent per day. If the length is 2, 4, 6, 8 cm on successive days the growth is arithmetic; if it is 2, 4, 8, 16 it is geometric.

where: growth rate, elongation per unit time

formulas.expr: W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub> e<sup>rt</sup> (geometric or exponential growth)
where: initial size at the beginning of the period

formulas.expr: Absolute growth rate = total growth per unit time; Relative growth rate = growth per unit time per unit initial parameter
where: 5 → 10 cm<sup>2</sup>: absolute 5 cm<sup>2</sup>, relative 100 per cent
50 → 55 cm<sup>2</sup>: absolute 5 cm<sup>2</sup>, relative 10 per cent

sections.tip: In arithmetic growth one daughter cell divides and the other differentiates; in geometric growth both keep dividing. State this cell-level difference first, then the equation, then the shape of the graph. That order matches the marking scheme.

sections.heading: 13.1.5 Conditions for Growth
sections.body:
This is a short section but it is a ready-made 2-mark or 3-mark question: 'What are the necessary conditions for growth?' NCERT names them in one paragraph and you should reproduce every item.

Water, oxygen and nutrients are the very essential elements for growth. The plant cells grow in size by cell enlargement, which in turn requires water. Turgidity of cells helps in extension growth: a cell that has taken in water pushes on its wall and stretches it, which is why wilted plants stop elongating. Water also provides the medium for enzymatic activities needed for growth. Oxygen helps in releasing metabolic energy essential for growth activities through respiration. Nutrients (macro and micro essential elements) are required by plants for the synthesis of protoplasm and act as a source of energy.

Every plant organism can grow only within a suitable range of temperature; an optimum temperature is needed, and a deviation from it could be detrimental to survival. Finally, environmental signals such as light and gravity affect certain phases or stages of growth. Light does not just supply energy for photosynthesis; it also acts as a signal (phototropism, the greening of a seedling), and gravity orients roots and shoots (geotropism).

A neat way to write the answer is a list of five: water (turgidity plus medium for enzymes), oxygen (metabolic energy), nutrients (protoplasm synthesis and energy source), optimum temperature, and light and gravity as environmental signals for particular phases. Link each to why it is needed; a bare list earns half the marks.

formulas.expr: Conditions for growth: water, oxygen, nutrients (essential); optimum temperature; light and gravity (affect certain phases)
where: turgidity for extension growth; medium for enzyme action

sections.tip: Mention turgidity by name when explaining the role of water. It is the one word the marking scheme looks for.

sections.heading: 13.2 Differentiation, Dedifferentiation and Redifferentiation
sections.body:
These three definitions appear in NCERT exercise question 1 and in nearly every school paper, so learn them in NCERT's own words and keep the examples attached.

Differentiation. The cells derived from the root apical and shoot apical meristems and the cambium differentiate and mature to perform specific functions. This act leading to maturation is termed differentiation. During differentiation cells undergo few to major structural changes both in their cell walls and in the protoplasm. For example, to form a tracheary element the cells lose their protoplasm and develop very strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls, so that they can carry water to long distances even under negative pressure. Differentiation makes a cell specialised for a job and it usually means the cell stops dividing.

Dedifferentiation. Plants show another interesting phenomenon: living differentiated cells that have lost the capacity to divide can regain it under certain conditions. This is dedifferentiation. NCERT's examples are the formation of the interfascicular cambium and the cork cambium (phellogen) from fully differentiated parenchyma cells. In secondary growth, parenchyma cells of the medullary rays between the vascular bundles start dividing again to form the interfascicular cambium; cortical parenchyma dedifferentiates to form the cork cambium. Wound healing and callus formation in tissue culture are the same idea.

Redifferentiation. While doing so (after dedifferentiation), such cells or tissues can divide and produce cells that once again lose the capacity to divide but mature to perform specific functions, that is, they redifferentiate. The secondary xylem and secondary phloem cut off by the interfascicular cambium, and the cork cells cut off by the cork cambium, are redifferentiated cells.

Put the three in a chain to remember them: meristematic cell → (differentiation) → mature parenchyma → (dedifferentiation) → cambium that divides again → (redifferentiation) → secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork.

Growth and differentiation are open. Recall that the growth in plants is open, meaning that new cells are always being added by the meristem. Differentiation in plants is also open, because cells or tissues arising out of the same meristem have different structures at maturity. The final structure at maturity of a cell or tissue is also determined by the location of the cell within the organ. For example, cells positioned away from the root apical meristem differentiate as root cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis. The same meristem, different fates depending on position: that is what 'open' differentiation means, and it is the answer to NCERT exercise question 6.

formulas.expr: Meristematic cell → differentiation → mature cell (e.g. tracheary element loses protoplasm, gains lignocellulosic secondary wall) → dedifferentiation → interfascicular cambium / cork cambium from parenchyma → redifferentiation → secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork
where: cells from the same meristem mature into different structures depending on position (root cap vs epidermis)

sections.tip: Always attach the examples: tracheary element for differentiation, interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma for dedifferentiation, secondary xylem and phloem for redifferentiation. Definitions without examples get 1 mark out of 2.

sections.heading: 13.3 Development and plasticity
sections.body:
Development is a term that includes all the changes an organism goes through during its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence. NCERT gives the sequence in Fig. 13.6 as a flow: a seed germinates into a seedling, the seedling grows into a mature plant, which flowers, produces fruits and seeds, and finally ages and dies (senescence). Development is the sum of growth and differentiation. The diagrammatic representation of the sequence of processes constituting the development of a cell of a higher plant is also shown: cell division → cell enlargement (growth) → differentiation → maturation → senescence and death.

Plasticity. Plants follow different pathways in response to environment or phases of life to form different kinds of structures. This ability is called plasticity. The NCERT examples must be quoted exactly. Heterophylly in cotton, coriander and larkspur: in these plants the leaves of the juvenile plant are different in shape from those of the mature plant. This is plasticity driven by the phase of life. In buttercup (Ranunculus), the leaves produced in air are different in shape from those produced in water. This is plasticity driven by the environment; the submerged leaves are finely dissected while the aerial leaves are broad and lobed. NCERT Fig. 13.7 shows both cases and it is worth a small sketch in a 3-mark answer.

Plasticity is why the same genotype can look different in different surroundings, and it is one reason plant development is described as open.

Factors controlling growth and development. Development in plants (i.e. both growth and differentiation) is under the control of intrinsic and extrinsic factors. The intrinsic factors are of two kinds: intracellular (genetic, the genome of the cell) and intercellular (chemical, the plant growth regulators). The extrinsic factors include light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition etc. The rest of the chapter deals with the intercellular intrinsic factors, the plant growth regulators.

formulas.expr: Development = growth + differentiation; sequence: seed → germination → seedling → mature plant → flowering → fruit and seed → senescence → death
Plasticity: heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur (juvenile vs mature leaves); buttercup leaves in air vs water
where: different leaf forms on the same plant

sections.tip: Cotton, coriander and larkspur are the phase-of-life examples; buttercup is the environment example. Do not mix them, and do not write 'lotus' or 'water hyacinth', which are not in NCERT.

sections.heading: 13.4 Plant Growth Regulators: 13.4.1 Characteristics and chemical nature
sections.body:
The plant growth regulators (PGRs) are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition. Because they are so varied chemically, they are grouped by their chemical class, and this grouping is a regular MCQ. They could be: indole compounds (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA); adenine derivatives (N6-furfurylamino purine, kinetin); derivatives of carotenoids (abscisic acid, ABA); terpenes (gibberellic acid, GA3); or gases (ethylene, C2H4). PGRs are variously described as plant growth substances, plant hormones or phytohormones.

Do not call them hormones in the animal sense without a caveat. Animal hormones are made in a gland and travel in blood to a distant target; PGRs are made in many tissues, act at very low concentrations, and often act near where they are made. The word 'regulator' is deliberate.

Two groups by activity. NCERT divides PGRs into two groups based on their functions in a living plant body. One group is involved in growth-promoting activities, such as cell division, cell enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting and seed formation; these are the plant growth promoters: auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins. The PGRs of the other group play an important role in plant responses to wounds and to stresses of biotic and abiotic origin; they are also involved in various growth-inhibiting activities such as dormancy and abscission. The PGR abscisic acid belongs to this group of growth inhibitors. The gaseous PGR, ethylene, could fit either of the groups, but it is largely an inhibitor of growth activities.

So the five groups are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid (this is the first half of NCERT exercise question 4). Learn the pairing 'name, chemical class, example' as a table because MCQs test it in every direction: which PGR is a terpene (GA3), which is a carotenoid derivative (ABA), which is an adenine derivative (kinetin, zeatin), which is an indole (IAA), which is a gas (ethylene).

formulas.expr: Chemical nature of PGRs: indole compounds (IAA); adenine derivatives (kinetin, N<sup>6</sup>-furfurylamino purine); carotenoid derivatives (ABA); terpenes (GA<sub>3</sub>); gases (ethylene C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>)
where: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins: cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting, seed formation
ABA: dormancy, abscission, responses to wounds and biotic/abiotic stress; ethylene fits both but is largely an inhibitor

sections.tip: Kinetin is N<sup>6</sup>-furfurylamino purine, an adenine (purine) derivative. ABA is derived from carotenoids, not from adenine. These two are the most swapped pair in MCQs.

sections.heading: 13.4.2 The Discovery of Plant Growth Regulators
sections.body:
Interestingly, all five major groups of PGRs were discovered accidentally, and each discovery has a plant, a scientist and an observation attached. Questions pair any two of these, so learn all three for each.

Auxin. The discovery of the first PGR began with the observations of Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin that the coleoptiles of canary grass responded to unilateral illumination by growing towards the light source (phototropism). After a series of experiments it was concluded that the tip of the coleoptile was the site of transmittable influence that caused the bending of the entire coleoptile (NCERT Fig. 13.8). F.W. Went (1928) isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings: he placed cut tips on agar blocks, and the agar block alone, placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile, made it bend, proving a diffusible chemical was responsible. The name auxin is from the Greek auxein, to grow.

Gibberellin. The 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice seedlings was caused by a fungal pathogen, Gibberella fujikuroi. Infected seedlings grew abnormally tall and thin and fell over. E. Kurosawa reported the appearance of the disease symptoms in uninfected rice seedlings when they were treated with sterile filtrates of the fungus. The active substances were later identified as gibberellic acid.

Cytokinin. F. Skoog and his co-workers observed that from the internodal segments of tobacco stems the callus (a mass of undifferentiated cells) proliferated only if, in addition to auxins, the nutrient medium was supplemented with one of the following: extracts of vascular tissues, yeast extract, coconut milk or DNA. Skoog and Miller later identified and crystallised the cytokinesis-promoting active substance that they termed kinetin. The source was autoclaved herring sperm DNA, a detail NEET likes.

Abscisic acid. During the mid-1960s, three independent researches reported the purification and chemical characterisation of three different kinds of inhibitors: inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin. Later all three were proved to be chemically identical, and the compound was named abscisic acid (ABA). Note the three roles hidden in the three names: growth inhibition, abscission and dormancy.

Ethylene. H.H. Cousins confirmed the release of a volatile substance from ripened oranges that hastened the ripening of stored unripened bananas. Later this volatile substance was identified as ethylene, a gaseous PGR.

In a 5-mark question on the discoveries, write five short paragraphs with the scientist, the plant or organism, the observation and the substance, exactly in this order. In a 1-mark question the trap is usually the plant: canary grass for Darwin, oat for Went, rice for Kurosawa, tobacco callus and herring sperm DNA for Skoog and Miller, oranges and bananas for Cousins.

formulas.expr: Discovery pairs: Darwin (canary grass coleoptile, phototropism) and Went (oat coleoptile, auxin); Kurosawa (bakanae of rice, Gibberella fujikuroi, gibberellin); Skoog and Miller (tobacco callus, herring sperm DNA, kinetin); inhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin = ABA; Cousins (ripe oranges hasten ripening of bananas, ethylene)
where: protective sheath over the plumule of a grass seedling; the classical phototropism material
unorganised mass of dividing cells in tissue culture

sections.tip: Bakanae means 'foolish seedling'; the fungus is Gibberella fujikuroi and the scientist is Kurosawa, not Yabuta (who purified gibberellin later and is not in NCERT). Stick to NCERT names.

sections.heading: 13.4.3 Physiological effects of PGRs: Auxins
sections.body:
Auxins (from Greek auxein, to grow) were first isolated from human urine, a fact NCERT states and MCQs use. The term auxin is applied to the indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) and to other natural and synthetic compounds having certain growth-regulating properties. They are generally produced by the growing apices of the stems and roots, from where they migrate to the regions of their action. Auxins like IAA and indole butyric acid (IBA) have been isolated from plants; these are the natural auxins. NAA (naphthalene acetic acid) and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) are synthetic auxins. All these auxins have been used extensively in agricultural and horticultural practices.

The physiological effects, in NCERT order, are the answer to any 3-mark or 5-mark question on auxins:

  1. They help to initiate rooting in stem cuttings, an application widely used for plant propagation (nurseries dip cuttings in IBA or NAA powder).
  2. Auxins promote flowering, e.g. in pineapples.
  3. They help to prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote the abscission of older, mature leaves and fruits. Both halves of this sentence are needed; the second half is what makes it a good Assertion-Reason item.
  4. Apical dominance. In most higher plants the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds. Removal of the shoot tips (decapitation) usually results in the growth of lateral buds. This is widely applied in tea plantations and hedge-making, where bushes are kept dense by repeated pruning.
  5. Auxins also induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes (fruit formed without fertilisation, hence seedless).
  6. They are widely used as herbicides. 2,4-D is widely used to kill dicotyledonous weeds; it does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants. It is used to prepare weed-free lawns by gardeners.
  7. Auxin also controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division.

A note on concentration that helps with Assertion-Reason questions: auxin promotes shoot growth at a concentration that already inhibits root growth, which is why the same hormone can be read as a promoter in one organ and an inhibitor in another. For the exam, keep to the NCERT list above and quote pineapple, tomato, tea plantations and 2,4-D by name.

formulas.expr: Auxins: natural IAA, IBA; synthetic NAA, 2,4-D. Effects: rooting in cuttings; flowering in pineapple; prevent early fruit and leaf drop, promote abscission of old leaves and fruits; apical dominance (decapitation releases lateral buds, tea and hedges); parthenocarpy in tomato; herbicide 2,4-D kills dicot weeds, spares mature monocots; xylem differentiation; cell division
where: indole-3-acetic acid, the principal natural auxin
2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, synthetic auxin, herbicide for weed-free lawns

sections.tip: For 'name one natural and one synthetic auxin' write IAA and 2,4-D (or IBA and NAA). Writing 'auxin' as the natural one earns nothing.

sections.heading: 13.4.3 Physiological effects of PGRs: Gibberellins
sections.body:
Gibberellins are another kind of promotory PGR. There are more than 100 gibberellins reported from widely different organisms such as fungi and higher plants. They are denoted as GA1, GA2, GA3 and so on. Gibberellic acid (GA3) was one of the first gibberellins to be discovered and remains the most intensively studied form. All GAs are acidic, and chemically they are terpenes.

They produce a wide range of physiological responses in plants, and the NCERT list should be reproduced in order:

  1. Their ability to cause an increase in length of the axis is used to increase the length of grapes stalks, so that the bunch is looser and the berries are larger.
  2. Gibberellins cause fruits like apple to elongate and improve their shape.
  3. They also delay senescence, so that fruits can be left on the tree longer, which extends the market period.
  4. GA3 is used to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry (GA induces the aleurone layer of barley grain to produce amylase, which converts starch to sugar).
  5. Sugarcane stores carbohydrate as sugar in its stems; spraying sugarcane crop with gibberellins increases the length of the stem, thus increasing the yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre.
  6. Spraying juvenile conifers with GAs hastens the maturity period, thus leading to early seed production.
  7. Gibberellins also promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering) in beet, cabbages and many plants with rosette habit.

Bolting is a definition asked on its own: rosette plants like cabbage and beet have very short internodes in their vegetative stage; just before flowering the internodes elongate suddenly and the flowering stalk shoots up. GA applied to a rosette plant induces this 'bolting' even without the usual cold or long-day requirement, which is why the answer to 'which PGR would you use to bolt a rosette plant' is gibberellin.

Remember also that GA and ABA are antagonistic in many situations (seed germination for instance: GA promotes it, ABA inhibits it), which NCERT states at the end of the ABA section. GA3 applied to rice seedlings makes them grow abnormally tall, reproducing the bakanae symptom, which is part (a) of NCERT exercise question 8.

formulas.expr: Gibberellins (GA<sub>1</sub>, GA<sub>2</sub>, GA<sub>3</sub> ...; more than 100 known; acidic terpenes). Effects: elongate grape stalks; elongate and shape apples; delay senescence so fruit stays on tree; GA<sub>3</sub> speeds malting in brewing; sugarcane stem length and yield up to 20 tonnes per acre; early seed production in juvenile conifers; bolting in beet and cabbage (rosette plants)
where: sudden internode elongation just before flowering in rosette plants
gibberellic acid, the most studied gibberellin

sections.tip: Apples elongate and improve in shape with GA; grapes get longer stalks. Students often swap these two. Sugarcane is the yield example, 20 tonnes per acre.

sections.heading: 13.4.3 Physiological effects of PGRs: Cytokinins
sections.body:
Cytokinins have a specific effect on cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, which is where the name comes from. They were discovered as kinetin (a modified form of adenine, a purine) from the autoclaved herring sperm DNA. Kinetin does not occur naturally in plants. The search for natural substances with cytokinin-like activity led to the isolation of zeatin from corn kernels and coconut milk. Since the discovery of zeatin, several naturally occurring cytokinins and some synthetic compounds with cell-division-promoting activity have been identified.

Natural cytokinins are synthesised in regions where rapid cell division occurs, for example root apices, developing shoot buds and young fruits. Note that the root apex is a major site of synthesis; cytokinins made in the roots travel up in the xylem to the shoot.

The physiological effects listed in NCERT:

  1. They help to produce new leaves, chloroplasts in leaves, lateral shoot growth and adventitious shoot formation.
  2. Cytokinins help overcome apical dominance. Auxin from the apex suppresses lateral buds; cytokinin applied to the lateral buds lets them grow. The ratio of auxin to cytokinin decides the outcome, and the same ratio decides whether a tissue-culture callus makes roots (high auxin) or shoots (high cytokinin).
  3. They promote nutrient mobilisation, which helps in the delay of leaf senescence. A leaf treated with cytokinin stays green longer because nutrients are drawn towards it rather than exported out of it.

Two of the NCERT exercise items rest on cytokinin. Question 7(c), delay leaf senescence: cytokinin. Question 7(d), induce growth in axillary buds: cytokinin. Question 8(d), if you forget to add cytokinin to the culture medium: the callus will not divide and proliferate properly and no shoots will differentiate, because cytokinesis and shoot formation need cytokinin (Skoog's original observation).

formulas.expr: Cytokinins: kinetin (modified adenine, from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, synthetic); zeatin (natural, from corn kernels and coconut milk). Made in root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits. Effects: new leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoots; overcome apical dominance; nutrient mobilisation and delay of leaf senescence
where: division of the cytoplasm; the effect that named the group
high auxin favours roots, high cytokinin favours shoots in tissue culture

sections.tip: Auxin causes apical dominance; cytokinin overcomes it. Cytokinin delays senescence; ethylene and ABA promote it. Write these as opposing pairs and Assertion-Reason questions become easy.

sections.heading: 13.4.3 Physiological effects of PGRs: Ethylene
sections.body:
Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR. It is synthesised in large amounts by tissues undergoing senescence and by ripening fruits. Because it is a gas it diffuses through the air in a store or a basket, which is why one rotten fruit spoils the lot (NCERT exercise question 8(c)).

Effects of ethylene on plants include horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings. These three together are the classical 'triple response' of dark-grown seedlings, though NCERT does not use that name. Ethylene promotes senescence and abscission of plant organs, especially of leaves and flowers. Ethylene is highly effective in fruit ripening. It enhances the respiration rate during ripening of the fruits; this rise in the rate of respiration is called respiratory climactic. Ethylene breaks seed and bud dormancy, initiates germination in peanut seeds and sprouting of potato tubers. Ethylene promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation in deep-water rice plants, which helps the leaves and upper parts of the shoot remain above water. It also promotes root growth and root hair formation, thus helping the plants to increase their absorption surface.

Ethylene in agriculture. It is used to initiate flowering and for synchronising fruit-set in pineapples; it also induces flowering in mango. Since ethylene regulates so many physiological processes, it is one of the most widely used PGRs in agriculture. The most widely used compound as a source of ethylene is ethephon. Ethephon in an aqueous solution is readily absorbed and transported within the plant and releases ethylene slowly. Ethephon hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples and accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut). It promotes female flowers in cucumbers, thereby increasing the yield.

For a 5-mark answer on ethylene, group the effects: seedling effects (three), senescence and abscission, fruit ripening and respiratory climactic, dormancy-breaking (peanut, potato), elongation in deep-water rice, root growth and root hairs, and then the agricultural uses with ethephon (pineapple, mango, tomato, apple, thinning, cucumber). Fruit sellers ripen bananas with ethylene or by keeping a ripe fruit in the basket, a scenario the case-based question often uses.

formulas.expr: Ethylene (gas, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>; made by senescing tissues and ripening fruits). Effects: horizontal growth, axis swelling, apical hook in dicot seedlings; senescence and abscission; fruit ripening with respiratory climactic; breaks seed and bud dormancy (peanut germination, potato sprouting); internode and petiole elongation in deep-water rice; root growth and root hairs. Uses: flowering and fruit-set in pineapple, flowering in mango; ethephon ripens tomato and apple, thins cotton, cherry, walnut, gives female flowers in cucumber
where: the rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening caused by ethylene
the most widely used source of ethylene; absorbed in aqueous solution and releases ethylene slowly

sections.tip: Auxin promotes flowering in pineapple; ethylene initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapple. Both are correct and both are in NCERT; do not argue with the option, read what is asked.

sections.heading: 13.4.3 Physiological effects of PGRs: Abscisic acid, and how PGRs act together
sections.body:
As mentioned earlier, abscisic acid (ABA) was discovered for its role in regulating abscission and dormancy. But like other PGRs it also has other wide-ranging effects on plant growth and development. It acts as a general plant growth inhibitor and an inhibitor of plant metabolism. ABA inhibits seed germination. ABA stimulates the closure of stomata in the epidermis and increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of stresses. Therefore, it is also called the stress hormone. That single line is the full answer to NCERT exercise question 5 (why ABA is called the stress hormone): under water stress ABA is produced, it closes the stomata to cut water loss, and it raises the plant's tolerance to drought, salinity and cold.

ABA plays an important role in seed development, maturation and dormancy. By inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds to withstand desiccation and other factors unfavourable for growth. In most situations, ABA acts as an antagonist to GAs: GA promotes germination, growth of the axis and bolting; ABA inhibits germination and growth and keeps buds and seeds dormant. A seed that stays dormant through a dry summer and germinates only when it rains is showing the ABA and GA balance in action.

PGRs act together, and with the environment. NCERT closes the chapter with a point that is easy to skip and easy to ask. Many events in the life of a plant are affected by more than one PGR: dormancy in seeds and buds, abscission, senescence, apical dominance, and also seed germination, plant movements and flowering. The PGRs act in synergy (auxin and cytokinin together in callus growth) or in antagonism (ABA against GA in germination, auxin against cytokinin in apical dominance). Also, the roles of PGRs are of many kinds in a plant's life, and the effect seen depends on the concentration, the tissue and the presence of other PGRs, which is why it is difficult in an experiment to assign an observed effect to any single hormone (an NCERT exemplar question). In addition to the intrinsic control by PGRs and the genome, extrinsic factors such as light and temperature control flowering and other developmental events, which links this chapter back to the extrinsic factors listed in Section 13.3.

For the exam, the two lines to memorise for ABA are 'general growth inhibitor, inhibits metabolism and seed germination' and 'closes stomata, increases stress tolerance, stress hormone; seed dormancy and desiccation tolerance; antagonist of GA'.

formulas.expr: ABA (carotenoid derivative): general growth inhibitor; inhibits metabolism and seed germination; stimulates stomatal closure; increases stress tolerance (stress hormone); seed development, maturation, dormancy; desiccation tolerance; antagonist of GA
where: ABA, because it closes stomata and raises tolerance to drought and other stresses
ABA vs GA (germination, dormancy); auxin vs cytokinin (apical dominance)
auxin plus cytokinin in callus proliferation

sections.tip: ABA promotes dormancy and abscission; it does not cause ripening. Ethylene ripens. If an MCQ pairs ABA with fruit ripening, that option is the wrong one.

key_terms.definition: An irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts, or an individual cell, generally accompanied by metabolic processes (anabolic and catabolic) that occur at the expense of energy.
A group of cells at particular locations (root apex, shoot apex, lateral cambia) that retain the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate, so that plant growth is indeterminate and open.
Growth that stops once the organism or organ reaches a fixed size, as in animals or a leaf; contrasted with the indeterminate growth of the plant body as a whole.

The plant pattern in which new cells are always being added to the body by meristems, so growth continues throughout life; differentiation is also open because cells from the same meristem mature into different structures depending on position.
The increased growth per unit time. Absolute growth rate is total growth per unit time; relative growth rate is growth per unit time per unit initial parameter.

Growth in which, after mitosis, only one daughter cell keeps dividing while the other differentiates; a constant amount is added per unit time giving a straight line, L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + rt.

Growth in which both daughter cells keep dividing so size increases exponentially, W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup>; shows lag, log (exponential) and stationary phases and gives a sigmoid curve.
The S-shaped curve obtained when a growth parameter is plotted against time for an organism in a natural environment; lag phase, exponential phase, stationary phase.
The relative growth rate r in W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup>; a measure of the ability of the plant to produce new plant material.

The act leading to maturation of cells derived from meristems and cambium, involving structural changes in cell wall and protoplasm, e.g. a tracheary element losing its protoplasm and developing a lignocellulosic secondary wall.
The regaining of the capacity to divide by living differentiated cells that had lost it, e.g. parenchyma forming interfascicular cambium and cork cambium.

The process by which dedifferentiated cells divide and produce cells that once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions, e.g. secondary xylem and phloem from cambium.
All the changes an organism goes through during its life cycle from seed germination to senescence; the sum of growth and differentiation.

The ability of plants to follow different pathways in response to environment or phase of life to form different kinds of structures, e.g. heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur and in buttercup leaves in air and water.
The occurrence of leaves of different shapes on the same plant, either at different ages (cotton, coriander, larkspur) or in different environments (buttercup in air and water).

Small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition (indoles, adenine derivatives, carotenoid derivatives, terpenes, gases) that regulate growth and development; also called phytohormones or plant growth substances.
The inhibition of growth of lateral (axillary) buds by the growing apical bud, mediated by auxin; removal of the shoot tip (decapitation) releases the lateral buds.
Formation of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruit; induced by auxins, e.g. in tomatoes.
Sudden elongation of internodes just prior to flowering in rosette plants such as beet and cabbage; promoted by gibberellins.
The ageing phase of a plant or organ ending in death; promoted by ethylene and ABA, delayed by cytokinins (through nutrient mobilisation) and gibberellins (in fruits).
The shedding of leaves, flowers or fruits from the plant; promoted by ethylene and ABA and by auxin in old organs, prevented by auxin in young organs.
The rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening brought about by ethylene.
The most widely used compound as a source of ethylene; absorbed in aqueous solution, transported within the plant and releases ethylene slowly.
Abscisic acid, so called because it stimulates stomatal closure and increases the tolerance of plants to various stresses.

formula_sheet.name: Definition of growth
formula_sheet.expr: Irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ, part or cell, accompanied by metabolic processes at the expense of energy
formula_sheet.note: Say 'irreversible' and 'permanent'; swelling by water uptake alone is not growth.

formula_sheet.name: Meristems and kind of growth
formula_sheet.expr: Root and shoot apical meristems → primary growth (elongation); lateral meristems (vascular cambium, cork cambium) → secondary growth (girth) in dicots and gymnosperms
formula_sheet.note: Plant growth is indeterminate and open because meristems keep adding cells.

formula_sheet.name: Numbers for measurable growth
formula_sheet.expr: Maize root apical meristem: more than 17,500 cells per hour; watermelon cell: size up by 3,50,000 times; pollen tube: length; dorsiventral leaf: surface area
formula_sheet.note: Parameters: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume, cell number.

formula_sheet.name: Phases of growth
formula_sheet.expr: Meristematic (rich protoplasm, large nuclei, thin primary cellulosic walls, abundant plasmodesmata) → elongation (vacuolation, cell enlargement, new wall deposition) → maturation (wall thickening, protoplasmic modifications)
formula_sheet.note: Seen at the root tip from the apex backwards; root hairs in the maturation zone.

formula_sheet.name: Arithmetic growth
formula_sheet.expr: L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + rt; one daughter cell divides, the other differentiates; straight-line graph
formula_sheet.note: Example: a root elongating at a constant rate.

formula_sheet.name: Geometric growth
formula_sheet.expr: W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup>; both daughter cells keep dividing; lag, log (exponential), stationary phases; sigmoid curve
formula_sheet.note: r = relative growth rate = efficiency index; e = base of natural logarithms.

formula_sheet.name: Absolute vs relative growth rate
formula_sheet.expr: Absolute = total growth per unit time; relative = growth per unit time per unit initial size. Leaf A 5 → 10 cm<sup>2</sup> and leaf B 50 → 55 cm<sup>2</sup>: same absolute growth (5 cm<sup>2</sup>), relative growth 100 per cent vs 10 per cent
formula_sheet.note: Smaller leaf has the higher relative growth rate.

formula_sheet.name: Conditions for growth
formula_sheet.expr: Water (turgidity, medium for enzymes), oxygen (metabolic energy), nutrients (protoplasm, energy); optimum temperature; light and gravity affect certain phases
formula_sheet.note: Give the reason with each condition.

formula_sheet.name: Differentiation chain
formula_sheet.expr: Meristem → differentiation (tracheary element: loses protoplasm, lignocellulosic secondary wall) → dedifferentiation (parenchyma → interfascicular cambium, cork cambium) → redifferentiation (secondary xylem, phloem, cork)
formula_sheet.note: Growth and differentiation are both open; root cap vs epidermis from the same meristem.

formula_sheet.name: Plasticity examples
formula_sheet.expr: Heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur (juvenile vs mature leaves); buttercup leaves in air vs water
formula_sheet.note: First set is phase of life; buttercup is environment.

formula_sheet.name: Chemical nature of PGRs
formula_sheet.expr: Indole: IAA; adenine derivative: kinetin (N<sup>6</sup>-furfurylamino purine), zeatin; carotenoid derivative: ABA; terpene: GA<sub>3</sub>; gas: ethylene C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>
formula_sheet.note: Promoters: auxin, GA, cytokinin. Inhibitor: ABA. Ethylene fits both, mostly inhibitor.

formula_sheet.name: Discovery table
formula_sheet.expr: Auxin: Darwin (canary grass coleoptile, phototropism), Went (oat coleoptile tips); GA: Kurosawa, bakanae disease of rice, Gibberella fujikuroi; cytokinin: Skoog and Miller, kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA, tobacco callus; ABA: inhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin; ethylene: Cousins, ripe oranges ripening bananas
formula_sheet.note: All five discovered accidentally; auxin first isolated from human urine.

formula_sheet.name: Auxin effects
formula_sheet.expr: Rooting of cuttings; flowering in pineapple; prevents early leaf and fruit drop, promotes abscission of old ones; apical dominance; parthenocarpy in tomato; 2,4-D kills dicot weeds, spares monocots; xylem differentiation; cell division

formula_sheet.name: Gibberellin effects
formula_sheet.expr: Longer grape stalks; apples elongate and improve in shape; delay senescence; GA<sub>3</sub> speeds malting; sugarcane yield up to 20 tonnes per acre; early seed production in juvenile conifers; bolting in beet and cabbage
formula_sheet.note: More than 100 GAs; all acidic; GA<sub>3</sub> most studied.

formula_sheet.name: Cytokinin effects
formula_sheet.expr: New leaves, chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoots; overcome apical dominance; nutrient mobilisation delays leaf senescence
formula_sheet.note: Zeatin from corn kernels and coconut milk; made in root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits.

formula_sheet.name: Ethylene effects and uses
formula_sheet.expr: Horizontal growth, axis swelling, apical hook in dicot seedlings; senescence, abscission; fruit ripening, respiratory climactic; breaks seed and bud dormancy (peanut, potato); deep-water rice elongation; root growth and root hairs; pineapple fruit-set, mango flowering; ethephon: tomato and apple ripening, thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut; female flowers in cucumber
formula_sheet.note: Most widely used PGR in agriculture; made by senescing tissues and ripening fruits.

formula_sheet.name: ABA effects
formula_sheet.expr: General growth inhibitor; inhibits metabolism and seed germination; stomatal closure; stress tolerance (stress hormone); seed development, maturation, dormancy; desiccation tolerance; antagonist of GA

diagrams.title: Root tip showing the three phases of growth (NCERT Fig. 13.2)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical root tip with a rounded root cap at the bottom. Above it mark three horizontal bands and label them from the tip upwards: meristematic zone (region of cell division), zone of elongation and zone of maturation. Draw a few root hairs on the maturation zone. Beside each zone write one feature of its cells: dense protoplasm and large nuclei with thin walls in the meristematic zone; enlarged vacuolated cells in the elongation zone; thick-walled mature cells in the maturation zone. Marking points: root cap, the three labelled zones in the right order, root hairs.

diagrams.title: Constant linear growth: arithmetic growth curve (NCERT Fig. 13.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes with time on the x-axis and length (or height) on the y-axis. Draw a straight line rising from a point on the y-axis (L<sub>0</sub>) at a constant slope. Write the equation L<sub>t</sub> = L<sub>0</sub> + rt beside it and label the slope as r, the growth rate. Below the graph write one line: one daughter cell divides, the other differentiates, so a fixed amount is added per unit time. Marking points: labelled axes, straight line starting at L<sub>0</sub>, equation, one-line explanation.

diagrams.title: Sigmoid growth curve of geometric growth (NCERT Fig. 13.4)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw axes with time on the x-axis and growth (size or number) on the y-axis. Draw an S-shaped curve: nearly flat at first, then rising steeply, then flattening. Label the three parts lag phase, log or exponential phase, and stationary phase. Optionally draw the arithmetic straight line on the same axes for comparison and label the two curves 'geometric' and 'arithmetic' as in NCERT. Write W<sub>1</sub> = W<sub>0</sub>e<sup>rt</sup> and note that both daughter cells keep dividing. Marking points: labelled axes, correct S shape, three phases named in order, equation.

diagrams.title: Absolute and relative growth: the two leaves (NCERT Fig. 13.5)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two leaves side by side, a small leaf A and a large leaf B, at 'time 1'. Below draw the same two leaves at 'time 2', each slightly bigger. Write the areas: A 5 cm<sup>2</sup> → 10 cm<sup>2</sup>, B 50 cm<sup>2</sup> → 55 cm<sup>2</sup>. Add two lines under the sketch: absolute growth of both = 5 cm<sup>2</sup>; relative growth of A = 100 per cent, of B = 10 per cent. Marking points: both leaves at two times, the four areas, the two comparison lines.

diagrams.title: Plasticity: heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur and buttercup (NCERT Fig. 13.7)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two rows. Top row: a young larkspur (or coriander) plant with simple, less divided leaves next to a mature plant of the same species with finely dissected leaves; label 'juvenile leaves' and 'mature leaves' and write 'heterophylly due to phase of life: cotton, coriander, larkspur'. Bottom row: a buttercup plant with the water line drawn across it; draw finely dissected thread-like leaves below the water and broad lobed leaves above it; label 'submerged leaves' and 'aerial leaves' and write 'heterophylly due to environment: buttercup'. Marking points: both examples, correct leaf shapes, the two causes named.

diagrams.title: Darwin's and Went's coleoptile experiments on phototropism and auxin (NCERT Fig. 13.8)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a row of canary grass or oat coleoptiles with a light source arrow from one side. First: intact coleoptile bending towards light. Second: tip removed, no bending. Third: tip covered by an opaque cap, no bending. Fourth: base covered but tip exposed, bending. Then Went's step: draw a cut tip placed on an agar block, the block placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile in the dark, and the coleoptile bending away from the side carrying the block. Label 'tip is the site of the transmittable influence' and 'auxin diffuses into the agar'. Marking points: light direction, the four treatments with their result, the agar block experiment.

diagrams.title: Apical dominance and its release by decapitation
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two shoots side by side. Left: an intact shoot with an apical bud at the top and small suppressed axillary buds in the leaf axils; write 'auxin from the apex inhibits lateral buds'. Right: the same shoot with the tip cut off (mark the cut with a line) and the axillary buds grown out into side branches; write 'decapitation releases lateral buds'. Add a note that cytokinin applied to the buds also overcomes apical dominance, and the application: tea plantations and hedges are pruned to make them bushy. Marking points: apical bud, axillary buds, the cut, side branches, the auxin and cytokinin labels.

diagrams.title: Effects of ethylene on a dark-grown dicot seedling
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two pea or bean seedlings grown in the dark. Left, control: a tall, thin, straight seedling with a slight hook. Right, with ethylene: a short seedling with a swollen, thick axis, growing horizontally rather than straight up, with an exaggerated apical hook. Label the three effects: horizontal growth, swelling of the axis, apical hook formation. Under the drawing write that ethylene is a gas produced by senescing tissues and ripening fruits. Marking points: the two seedlings compared and the three effects labelled.

diagrams.title: Structures of the five PGRs (NCERT Fig. 13.9)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the five structures as simple outlines with names beneath: IAA as an indole ring (a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing N) with a CH<sub>2</sub>COOH side chain; GA<sub>3</sub> as a four-ring terpene skeleton with a lactone ring and a COOH; zeatin as a purine (adenine) with a side chain on N<sup>6</sup>; ethylene as H<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>; ABA as a six-membered ring with a side chain ending in COOH (a carotenoid derivative). Beside each write its chemical class: indole, terpene, adenine derivative, gas, carotenoid derivative. Examiners rarely demand exact structures; the class labels and ethylene's formula are the marks.

ncert_questions.q: Define growth, differentiation, development, dedifferentiation, redifferentiation, determinate growth, meristem and growth rate.
ncert_questions.a:
Growth: an irreversible permanent increase in size of an organ or its parts or even of an individual cell, generally accompanied by metabolic processes that occur at the expense of energy.

Differentiation: the process by which cells derived from the root apical and shoot apical meristems and the cambium mature to perform specific functions, undergoing structural changes in cell wall and protoplasm, e.g. formation of tracheary elements.

Development: all the changes an organism goes through during its life cycle from germination of the seed to senescence; the sum of growth and differentiation.

Dedifferentiation: the regaining of the capacity to divide by living differentiated cells that had lost it, e.g. formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma.

Redifferentiation: the process in which dedifferentiated cells divide and produce cells that once again lose the capacity to divide and mature to perform specific functions, e.g. secondary xylem and phloem.

Determinate growth: growth that stops after the organ or organism reaches a certain size, as in animals and in a leaf or a flower; contrasted with the indeterminate growth of the plant body.

Meristem: a group of cells at the root apex, shoot apex and lateral positions (cambium) that retain the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate, giving the plant its open form of growth.

Growth rate: the increased growth per unit time; it may be expressed as absolute growth rate (total growth per unit time) or relative growth rate (growth per unit time per unit initial size).

ncert_questions.q: Why is not any one parameter good enough to demonstrate growth throughout the life of a flowering plant?
ncert_questions.a: Growth at the cellular level is basically an increase in the amount of protoplasm, which cannot be measured directly, so we measure growth through parameters such as increase in fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number. Different organs and stages of a flowering plant grow in different ways, so no single parameter fits all of them: a maize root apical meristem produces more than 17,500 new cells per hour (cell number), a watermelon cell may enlarge up to 3,50,000 times (volume), a pollen tube grows in length, a dorsiventral leaf grows in surface area, a tuber grows in dry weight. Fresh weight changes with water content and may not reflect true growth, while dry weight cannot be measured without destroying the plant. Because each parameter suits only one kind of organ or one stage of life, a combination of parameters, chosen to suit the organ and stage, is needed to demonstrate growth throughout the plant's life.

ncert_questions.q: Describe briefly: (a) Arithmetic growth (b) Geometric growth (c) Sigmoid growth curve (d) Absolute and relative growth rates.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Arithmetic growth: after mitotic cell division only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates and matures. A constant amount is added per unit time, so a plot of length against time is a straight line. Example: a root elongating at a constant rate. Expressed as Lt = L0 + rt, where Lt is length at time t, L0 the length at time zero and r the growth rate.

(b) Geometric growth: both daughter cells of mitosis retain the ability to divide, so the number (or size) multiplies. Initial growth is slow (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase), then it slows as nutrients become limiting (stationary phase). Expressed as W1 = W0ert, where W1 is the final size, W0 the initial size, r the relative growth rate (efficiency index), t the time and e the base of natural logarithms.

(c) Sigmoid growth curve: when a growth parameter of an organism growing in a natural environment is plotted against time, an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve is obtained, made of the lag phase, the exponential phase and the stationary phase. It is characteristic of all cells, tissues and organs of a plant.

(d) Absolute and relative growth rates: absolute growth rate is the measurement and comparison of total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate is the growth of the given system per unit time expressed on a common basis, per unit initial parameter. Two leaves that both add 5 cm2 in the same time have the same absolute growth, but the leaf that went from 5 to 10 cm2 has a relative growth of 100 per cent while the one that went from 50 to 55 cm2 has only 10 per cent.

ncert_questions.q: List five main groups of natural plant growth regulators. Write a note on discovery, physiological functions and agricultural/horticultural applications of any one of them.
ncert_questions.a:
The five main groups are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid.

Note on auxins. Discovery: Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin observed that coleoptiles of canary grass bend towards unilateral light (phototropism) and concluded that the tip is the site of a transmittable influence. F.W. Went isolated auxin from the tips of oat coleoptiles. Auxin was first isolated from human urine. Physiological functions: auxins (natural IAA and IBA, synthetic NAA and 2,4-D) are produced by growing apices of stems and roots and migrate to their site of action. They initiate rooting in stem cuttings, promote flowering (pineapple), prevent early fruit and leaf drop but promote abscission of older leaves and fruits, cause apical dominance (the apical bud inhibits lateral buds; decapitation releases them), induce parthenocarpy (tomato), control xylem differentiation and help in cell division. Applications: rooting of cuttings in plant propagation; 2,4-D as a herbicide to kill dicot weeds and prepare weed-free lawns without harming monocots; pruning of tea plantations and hedges to exploit apical dominance; production of seedless tomatoes; inducing flowering in pineapple; preventing premature fruit drop in orchards.

ncert_questions.q: Why is abscisic acid also known as stress hormone?
ncert_questions.a: Abscisic acid (ABA) is produced in larger amounts when a plant faces stress such as drought, high salinity or cold. It stimulates the closure of stomata in the epidermis, which reduces water loss by transpiration, and it increases the tolerance of the plant to various kinds of stresses. It also acts as a general growth inhibitor, induces dormancy of seeds and buds so they can withstand desiccation and other unfavourable conditions, and inhibits seed germination in adverse conditions. Because it helps the plant survive stress, ABA is called the stress hormone.

ncert_questions.q: 'Both growth and differentiation in higher plants are open.' Comment.
ncert_questions.a: Growth in higher plants is open because meristems (root apical, shoot apical and lateral) retain the capacity to divide throughout the life of the plant; new cells are always being added to the body, so growth is indeterminate and continues as long as the plant lives. Differentiation is also open because the cells or tissues arising out of the same meristem have different structures at maturity, and the final structure of a cell is determined by its location within the organ. For example, cells positioned away from the root apical meristem differentiate as root cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis; cells from the same shoot apical meristem become xylem, phloem, parenchyma or epidermis depending on their position. Thus neither the amount of growth nor the fate of the cells is fixed in advance, which is what 'open' means.

ncert_questions.q: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to: (a) induce rooting in a twig (b) quickly ripen a fruit (c) delay leaf senescence (d) induce growth in axillary buds (e) 'bolt' a rosette plant (f) induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Induce rooting in a twig: auxin (IBA or NAA).
(b) Quickly ripen a fruit: ethylene (applied as ethephon).
(c) Delay leaf senescence: cytokinin.
(d) Induce growth in axillary buds: cytokinin (it overcomes apical dominance).
(e) 'Bolt' a rosette plant: gibberellin (GA3).
(f) Induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves: abscisic acid.

ncert_questions.q: What would be expected to happen if: (a) GA<sub>3</sub> is applied to rice seedlings (b) dividing cells stop differentiating (c) a rotten fruit gets mixed with unripe fruits (d) you forget to add cytokinin to the culture medium.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The rice seedlings will show abnormal elongation of the stem and grow excessively tall and thin, the bakanae (foolish seedling) symptom, because gibberellins cause increase in length of the axis.
(b) If dividing cells stop differentiating there will be no formation of mature tissues and organs; the cells will remain a mass of undifferentiated, dividing cells (a callus), like a tumour, and no specialised functions will be performed.
(c) The rotten fruit releases ethylene, a gaseous PGR that promotes ripening and senescence; the unripe fruits will ripen quickly and then over-ripen and spoil.
(d) Without cytokinin the cells of the callus will not divide (cytokinesis is promoted by cytokinins) and no shoots will differentiate, since shoot formation requires cytokinin along with auxin; the culture will fail to proliferate and to form new plantlets.

ncert_questions.q: What are the structural characteristics of the cells of the meristematic phase at the root tip? How do the cells of the elongation and maturation phases differ from them?
ncert_questions.a: Cells of the meristematic phase are constantly dividing. They are rich in protoplasm, have large conspicuous nuclei, and their cell walls are primary in nature, thin and cellulosic, with abundant plasmodesmatal connections. Cells of the phase of elongation, just proximal to the meristem, show increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new cell wall deposition; they are no longer dividing but growing in size. Cells of the phase of maturation, further from the apex, have attained their maximal size with wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications, and have become the mature tissues of the root (root hairs form in this zone).

ncert_questions.q: Plants differ from animals in having an open form of growth. Explain what this means and how it is related to plasticity.
ncert_questions.a: Animals grow to a fixed size and then stop (determinate growth). Plants retain meristems throughout life, and the cells of the meristems keep dividing and adding new cells to the body, so plant growth is indeterminate; this pattern, in which new cells are always being added, is the open form of growth. Because the plant keeps forming new organs all through its life, it can respond to its environment or to its phase of life by forming different kinds of structures at different times, which is plasticity. For example, cotton, coriander and larkspur produce juvenile leaves of a different shape from their mature leaves (heterophylly), and buttercup produces different leaves in air and in water. Open growth makes such changing responses possible.

ncert_questions.q: Does the growth rate of a plant remain constant throughout its life? Give reasons.
ncert_questions.a: No. The growth of an organism in a natural environment follows a sigmoid curve: growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase) while nutrients are plentiful and both daughter cells keep dividing, and then slows down and becomes stationary as nutrient supply becomes limiting and the plant matures and ages. Different organs also grow at different rates and at different times, and extrinsic factors such as water, temperature, light and nutrients change through the seasons. Hence the growth rate varies through the life of the plant.

ncert_questions.q: While experimenting with plant growth regulators, why is it difficult to assign any effect seen to any single hormone?
ncert_questions.a: Several reasons make it difficult. (i) Most events in a plant's life, such as dormancy, abscission, senescence, apical dominance, seed germination and flowering, are controlled by more than one PGR acting together. (ii) PGRs act in synergy (auxin and cytokinin together cause callus proliferation) or in antagonism (ABA opposes GA in germination; cytokinin opposes auxin in apical dominance), so the observed response is the net result of several PGRs. (iii) The response depends on concentration: the same auxin promotes shoot growth and inhibits root growth. (iv) The response depends on the tissue and its stage: auxin prevents abscission of young leaves but promotes abscission of old ones. (v) Applying one PGR often changes the synthesis or transport of others (auxin can induce ethylene synthesis). (vi) Extrinsic factors such as light and temperature also act along with PGRs. Because of these interactions, an effect seen after treatment cannot be attributed to a single hormone with certainty.

ncert_questions.q: A gardener prunes his hedge plants regularly to make them dense. Name the phenomenon involved and the hormone responsible for it.
ncert_questions.a: The phenomenon is apical dominance. Auxin produced by the apical bud inhibits the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds; when the gardener removes the shoot tips (decapitation), the lateral buds grow out into branches and the hedge becomes dense. Cytokinins help overcome apical dominance.

pyq.q: Which of the following plant growth regulators is a gas?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Ethylene (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) is the only gaseous PGR. ABA is a carotenoid derivative, GA<sub>3</sub> a terpene and zeatin an adenine derivative.

pyq.solution: The disease, caused by the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, was reproduced by Kurosawa with sterile fungal filtrates; the active substance was gibberellic acid.

pyq.q: Which one of the following is a synthetic auxin widely used as a herbicide to kill dicotyledonous weeds?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid is a synthetic auxin that kills dicot weeds and does not affect mature monocots; IAA and IBA are natural auxins, zeatin is a cytokinin.

pyq.q: Kinetin, the first cytokinin, was obtained from
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Skoog and Miller crystallised kinetin from autoclaved herring sperm DNA. Zeatin, the natural cytokinin, came from corn kernels and coconut milk.

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The sigmoid curve begins with a slow lag phase, then the rapid log (exponential) phase, and finally the stationary phase when nutrients become limiting.

pyq.q: Which plant growth regulator promotes bolting in rosette plants such as cabbage and beet?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Gibberellins cause internode elongation just prior to flowering (bolting) in beet, cabbage and other rosette plants.

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT states more than 17,500 new cells per hour. The figure 3,50,000 is the factor by which a watermelon cell can increase in size.
